section_summary: Pages 1–28 continue a State Department register of papers concerning American exports of arms, scrap metal, petroleum, machinery, and other strategic materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War, including public protests, congressional inquiries, diplomatic reports, and proposed neutrality legislation. Pages 29–64 contain selected underlying records: correspondence about applying the Neutrality Act, a Shanghai consular despatch, and a major San Diego petition campaign opposing shipments of scrap iron and war materials to Japan. The section ends amid the petition’s signature sheets, which continue beyond page 64.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Army Equipment—Japan, entries 440–669
subfiles.doc_type: archival list of papers / file register
subfiles.about: A continued chronological register summarizes correspondence, memoranda, diplomatic reports, petitions, and legislative inquiries concerning American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The register records a large wave of protests against exporting scrap iron, petroleum, aircraft, machinery, munitions, and other strategic materials to Japan. It also lists State Department replies explaining the Neutrality Act, congressional requests for information, diplomatic reporting from East Asia and Europe, and discussions with American businesses. Entries extend from autumn 1938 into May 1939 and refer to proposed embargoes, picketing of Japanese ships, the Nine-Power Treaty, and bills such as H.R. 3419.

subfiles.title: Merrill Fowler Clarke to Cordell Hull urging an embargo on materials usable in war
subfiles.about: Clarke urges the government to impose a presidential embargo on materials and machinery aiding Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Clarke argues that American machine tools, trucks, and metals have made the United States Japan’s most important partner in prosecuting the war. He contends that China’s loss of supply routes through Hong Kong and Canton removes a principal objection to applying stronger neutrality measures. Drawing on reports from Americans returned from Shanghai, he asks Hull to explore a presidential embargo and also regrets Hull’s inability to address the Connecticut Council of Churches.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Merrill Fowler Clarke on the Neutrality Act
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the President has not proclaimed a state of war between China and Japan and describes the legal limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that the President exercised the discretion granted by the Neutrality Act of May 1, 1937 when he declined to declare that a state of war existed. It emphasizes that the act could prohibit only formally enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war, not ordinary commodities such as scrap metal. The Department reports that recent arms-export licenses for Japan were small and notes that manufacturers had substantially complied with its July 1 request not to encourage aerial bombing of civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Delivery of a State Department letter to Reverend John C. Hawk
subfiles.from: C. E. Gauss, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Gauss reports arrangements for safely delivering a State Department letter to missionary John C. Hawk in Wuhing, Chekiang.
subfiles.summary: The Shanghai consulate acknowledges the Department’s instruction of September 8 enclosing a letter for Reverend John C. Hawk. Because Hawk was then at Wuhing (Huchow), Chekiang, the letter was entrusted to Dr. John W. Cline, head of Hawk’s Methodist mission in Shanghai, for safe delivery.

subfiles.title: San Diego protest against shipments of scrap iron and war material to Japan
subfiles.from: W. J. Sherman and Kate H. Dewing, Peace Committee of San Diego and San Diego Branch of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: San Diego peace activists submit protests urging the administration to halt shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writers condemn the inconsistency between American criticism of Japan’s invasion of China and private American commerce that supplies Japan with the means to continue it. They argue that the administration should find a way to stop the trade, even though they recognize the legal and commercial complexities involved. The submission stresses goodwill toward the Japanese people while acknowledging American responsibility for helping equip Japan, and it includes a printed petition form.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the San Diego petition
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges a petition bearing 983 signatures against exports of scrap iron and war material to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges, by referral from the White House, the communication signed by Sherman and Kate H. Dewing. It identifies the enclosed petition as containing 983 signatures and opposing exports of scrap iron and war material to Japan. Yost refers Sherman to a Department reply of November 10 concerning a similar submission.

subfiles.title: San Diego petition with signature sheets against exports to Japan
subfiles.from: W. J. Sherman, Kate H. Dewing, and petition signers
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The Peace Committee of San Diego and the local WILPF branch submit a mass petition protesting shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cover letter repeats the argument that American private commerce was enabling Japan’s invasion and destruction in China despite official American disapproval. It asks the administration to reconcile this contradiction and halt strategic exports while maintaining that the protest is directed against aggressive policy rather than the Japanese people. The remaining pages are printed petition sheets signed principally by residents of San Diego and nearby California communities; the run of signatures is incomplete at page 64 and continues into the next section.
